stories.headline: Mullin calls Mamdani's anti-ICE rhetoric 'dangerous' following New York shooting
stories.note: Homeland Security's Markwayne Mullin hit back at Mayor Mamdani for trashing ICE right after an agent shooting in NYC, warning his words put officers at risk.
body: Homeland Security's Markwayne Mullin pushed back hard on Friday against New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who attacked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after ICE officers shot a man in the city on Thursday.
Mamdani responded to the shooting by repeating his call to abolish ICE, claiming the agency has "killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save."

At a press conference, Mullin said the mayor's language was reckless and asked who would remove criminals from New York's streets if ICE were gone. "His words are dangerous and incite hostility," Mullin said.

ICE enforcement official Marcos Charles said the man who was shot, Oscar Belgal, refused orders to get out of his vehicle, then rammed two government vehicles and drove toward other officers. Mullin added that officers didn't know a child was in the car, but that Belgal did.
Fox News noted this is a breaking story that's still developing.

Why it matters: Mamdani's push to abolish ICE gives Republicans a clear contrast on law and order, and it puts other Democrats in the spot of having to defend or distance themselves from New York's mayor.

stories.headline: Schumer digs in as progressive candidates withhold support for top Senate Dem
stories.note: Chuck Schumer insists he's staying on as leader, but several of his own party's Senate candidates won't commit to backing him.
body: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Politico he's running again to lead Senate Democrats, "Period," no matter how November turns out. He says his party has "wind in our sails" heading into the midterms.

But a number of the Democrats he's counting on to win key races aren't on board. Kansas candidate Adam Hamilton, running against Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, said again this week he won't back Schumer for leader, calling for new ideas, fresh leadership, and age and term limits.
Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan have also refused to commit to Schumer, even while taking money from the Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC closely tied to him.

The grumbling isn't new. Fox reports Democrats questioned Schumer's leadership twice last year over his handling of government shutdown fights, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan has openly called for "significant new leadership." Progressives, including El-Sayed, have floated Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen as a possible replacement, though he says he's focused only on the midterms.
Other Democrats are steering clear of the subject. Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut declined to say whether winning the Senate would strengthen Schumer's hand.

Why it matters: When a party's own candidates won't stand behind their leader weeks before an election, it signals division, and it hands Republicans an easy argument that Democrats are fighting each other instead of the issues.

stories.headline: Democrats are changing their transgender message. Republicans say they're just flip-flopping
stories.note: Democrats in tough races are suddenly running away from their past positions on trans athletes, and Republicans are calling out the election-season flip-flop.
body: Several Democrats in competitive races are now saying they oppose biological males in women's sports, and Republicans say it's a last-minute flip-flop. South Carolina Senate nominee Dr. Annie Andrews told Fox News Digital she opposes both, and says so in a new ad.

Her Republican opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, points to Andrews' opposition to a 2022 South Carolina law keeping transgender athletes off girls' school teams. At the time, Andrews called it "shameful legislation" and wrote that she would "always support trans youth."

Andrews isn't alone. Fox reports that Texas nominee James Talarico, Iowa nominee Josh Turek, Ohio Rep. Marcy Kaptur and North Carolina Rep. Don Davis have all shifted or softened their messaging. The NRCC noted Kaptur voted against the GOP's Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act in both 2023 and 2025.

The politics favor the GOP on this one. A Fox News poll last month found 76% of voters back banning biological men from women's sports, including 61% of Democrats. Republicans spent more than $200 million on the issue in 2024, and Trump has called it one of the party's best messages.

Democrats say they're just defining themselves before Republicans can. Democratic strategist Maria Cardona argued voters care more about costs like gas prices than culture issues. GOP strategist Colin Reed countered that voters should be skeptical of positions that change weeks before an election.
Why it matters: The scramble shows Democrats know they're on the wrong side of most voters here, and Republicans can point to the record to argue the new positions aren't sincere.

stories.headline: US Attorney calls out 'loud-mouth' California Dems as feds step in with Skid Row drug bust: 'They're lunatics'
stories.note: Federal agents swept Skid Row in a huge drug bust, and the top federal prosecutor there blamed California Democrats' soft-on-crime laws for letting it get this bad.
body: Federal and Los Angeles authorities carried out Operation Save Skid Row on Thursday, serving 28 arrest warrants and 44 search warrants aimed at the drug networks operating in the notorious neighborhood.

More than 100 law enforcement vehicles took part, and the arrests targeted members of several gangs, including the Main Street Crips, the Grape Street/Raymond Avenue Crips and the Pueblo Bishop Bloods.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told Fox News Digital that local police aren't the problem. He blamed Gov. Newsom's state, its legislature and outspoken Democratic members of Congress for weakening criminal laws and closing prisons, leaving little deterrence at the state level.

Essayli did credit Mayor Karen Bass for letting the LAPD join the operation. But he said people pushing to defund or disarm police are siding with the dealers who were arrested. "They're lunatics," he said.
He also tied the drug trade to the homelessness crisis, saying dealers keep people addicted and take their public assistance money, and vowed an end to open-air drug markets.

Why it matters: The bust shows the Trump administration stepping in where Democratic leaders haven't, and it gives Republicans a concrete example for their argument that California's policies have failed on crime.

stories.headline: DeSantis fraud crackdown drives nearly $1B spending plunge after providers billed impossible hours
stories.note: Gov. DeSantis' Medicaid fraud crackdown cut nearly $1 billion in projected spending after Florida caught providers billing more than 24 hours in a day.
body: Florida says its Medicaid fraud crackdown has cut projected yearly spending on one type of therapy by nearly $1 billion. Spending on Applied Behavior Analysis, a common autism therapy, was projected at $3.86 billion but is now expected to be $2.88 billion for fiscal 2026-27.

The state's Agency for Health Care Administration told Fox News Digital that it found providers billing every weekend and holiday for months, and some billing for more than 24 hours of services in a single day.

More than 220 providers have been kicked out of the program for fraud, waste or abuse, more than 260 have had payments restricted or suspended, and over 150 suspected fraud cases have gone to the attorney general in the past year.

Florida's approach is to stop bad claims before the money goes out, rather than chasing it afterward, matching a call from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The state is also screening for fake identities and hidden owners, has done 400 site visits since January, and has issued more than 1,000 adverse enrollment decisions.

DeSantis called it "the most significant Medicaid integrity initiative in the history of our state." The state noted officials credit the savings to a mix of fraud enforcement, managed care and utilization controls.
Why it matters: Florida's results stand in sharp contrast to the Medicaid fraud scandal in Democrat-run Minnesota, and they give Republicans a working model for protecting taxpayer money.

stories.headline: Dem who ripped rival's donor-fueled 'good life' dropped campaign cash on Disney, spouse travel
stories.note: Texas Democrat Vicente Gonzalez mocked a Republican for Disney trips on donor money, but his own campaign paid for Disney, Abu Dhabi and Zurich trips with his wife.
body: Democratic Texas Rep. Vicente Gonzalez once mocked Republican Mayra Flores for "living the good life on donor's resources" after her campaign reported Disney World payments. Now a Fox News Digital review of his own records shows something similar.

According to FEC filings, Gonzalez's campaign paid $1,122.76 to Walt Disney Resorts in March and May 2025, around the time he posted photos from a two-day Disney World trip with his wife. Fox reports nearly $20,000 in campaign spending tied to domestic and overseas trips with his wife.

That includes more than $13,000 for airfare and a luxury hotel in Abu Dhabi in late 2024, a trip Gonzalez called an "after campaign break" on social media, plus a Michelin-starred restaurant bill in Zurich, a five-star hotel in Rome and thousands more at upscale restaurants and resorts.

His campaign manager, Alex Philley, said every dollar was legal and publicly disclosed, and that the trips were tied to official business, including a Financial Services Committee trip and a meeting with the Pope. FEC rules let campaigns cover a spouse's travel only when it's tied to campaign or official duties.
Gonzalez is defending his South Texas seat against Republican Eric Flores in a race both parties are watching closely.
Why it matters: The hypocrisy charge could hurt Gonzalez in one of the GOP's best pickup chances in South Texas, where Republicans have been making big gains with Hispanic voters.

stories.headline: Schumer, Jeffries dodge Mamdani controversy as fellow New York Dem unloads
stories.note: Schumer and Jeffries are staying silent on Mamdani's Oct. 7 statement attacking Israel, even as fellow New York Democrat Dan Goldman called it reprehensible.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is under fire for his statement on the anniversary of Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel. His post briefly mentioned the attack but spent most of its length accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza and saying Americans' "tax dollars fund these war crimes."
Fox notes the statement didn't mention New York's Jewish community, which numbers close to 1 million people.
Democratic Rep. Dan Goldman blasted the mayor, calling it "a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack."

But the two most powerful Democrats in Congress, both New Yorkers, haven't said a word about it. Neither Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries answered Fox's requests for comment, though each released his own Oct. 7 statement.

Schumer called the attack the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Jeffries said the death of Palestinian civilians and devastation in Gaza were reprehensible and that U.S. policy in the region "must change dramatically," including support for a Palestinian state.

Why it matters: Democratic leaders' silence on their party's most prominent mayor shows how divided they are on Israel, and it lets Republicans argue the party's leadership won't stand up to its far left.
